Neurophysiology · Lecture 1

Introduction — The Sensory System

The sensory system provides information about the internal and external environment. Every sensation — a rise in temperature, pain, touch, pressure — is translated for us by this system.

All information reaches us through sense organs, which contain structures called receptors. A sense organ has a neural part (the sensory receptors) and a non-neural part. For any sensation to be perceived, the stimulus must reach the sensory receptors, which then relay it to a center in the spinal cord or brain, where it is interpreted.

Fig. The sensory system is made of sensory receptors + sensory pathways + sensory centres.

Roadmap
This lecture covers: Definition · Functions · Classification · Properties · Coding of sensory information. The ascending sensory pathways themselves are covered in the next lecture.
Concept

Definition of a Sensory Receptor

Definition
A sensory receptor is a special structure at the peripheral end of an afferent neuron, or a special structure at the dendritic end of a sensory neuron.

Because the receptor sits at the very end of the afferent pathway, it is the first point of contact between a physical/chemical stimulus and the nervous system. Everything the brain will eventually "feel" starts here.

"عبارة عن structure special بنلقاه في الـ end بتاعة الـ afferent... او في الـ end of the dendritic."
Concept

Functions of Sensory Receptors

Every receptor performs the same three jobs, in sequence, regardless of the modality:

1 · Detector

Detector

Detects a change in the internal or external environment — the first step, simply recognizing that a stimulus has occurred.

2 · Transducer

Transducer

Converts the various forms of stimulus energy into a local electrical signal called the receptor potential.

3 · Generator

Generator

Converts the receptor potential into an action potential. When action potentials reach the brain, we experience a sensation.

Why an action potential?
The brain only "understands" action potentials — every sensation arrives at the brain in the form of action potentials, which are then decoded using a specific coding system (see Coding of Sensory Information) to reveal whether the input was cold, heat, pain, touch, or pressure — much like a student ID number encodes name, department, batch, and semester.
Classification 1 of 3

By Type of Stimulus

Receptors are classified by the kind of energy that activates them into five types:

TypeAdequate stimulusSub-types / examples
MechanoreceptorsMechanical (touch, pressure, vibration)Proprioceptors (position, movement, rate of movement); Vestibular receptors (non-auditory — balance, position, movement)
ThermoreceptorsThermal — heat or coldSkin thermal receptors
ChemoreceptorsChemicalTaste & smell receptors; O₂/CO₂/H⁺ chemoreceptors; Osmoreceptors (detect change in ECF solute concentration — hypertonic / hypotonic / isotonic)
PhotoreceptorsElectromagnetic (light)Rods & cones in the retina
NociceptorsNoxious / tissue-damaging stimulus (not modality-specific)Free nerve endings — pain receptors
High-yield distinction
Nociceptors are unusual: they don't have one adequate stimulus. Any form of energy — mechanical, thermal, or chemical — will excite them if it is intense enough to cause tissue damage.
Classification 2 of 3

By Structure of the Receptor

Receptors are also classified by their anatomical form into three groups:

Must-know pairing
"مطلوب منكم تعرفوا كل واحد مسؤول من شنو بيستقبل شنو" — know exactly which receptor answers which stimulus: Pacinian → deep pressure / fast vibration · Meissner's → slow vibration · Merkel's discs → sustained pressure & touch · Ruffini → sustained pressure · Free nerve endings → pain & temperature.
Classification 3 of 3

By Site of the Event

ClassDetectsExample
TeleceptorsDistant events (name derived from "tele" = far)Visual, auditory, olfactory (smell) receptors — you cannot "taste" something far away, so taste is not teleceptive
ExteroceptorsStimuli from outside the bodyTouch receptors
InteroceptorsInternal stimuliChemoreceptors
Properties 1 of 3

Specificity

Definition
Each type of receptor is most sensitive to one specific form of energy, called its adequate stimulus.
ReceptorAdequate stimulus
Touch receptorsMechanical energy
Temperature receptorsThermal energy (heat / cold)
Visual receptorsElectromagnetic energy
Exception to the rule
A receptor can respond to a stimulus that is not its adequate stimulus — but only at a much higher threshold. Classic example: extreme mechanical pressure on a closed eye produces a sensation of light ("seeing stars") — the exact trick used in cartoons.

Müller's Law (Law of Specific Nerve Energies)

The sensory pathway from a given receptor to the cortex is specific. When that pathway is stimulated — by any means — it produces only one sensation: the one the receptor is specialised for, irrespective of the method of stimulation.

Analogy: you board a bus signed "Khartoum" from Port Sudan — no matter what happens along the way, that bus only ever arrives in Khartoum. Likewise, a pathway from a given receptor always delivers the same sensation, regardless of what triggered it.
Important exception
The adequate stimulus rule does not strictly apply to pain (nociceptors): any form of energy — mechanical, thermal, or chemical — can produce pain, as long as it is intense enough to cause tissue damage.
Properties 2 of 3

Excitability

Definition
Excitability is the ability of a receptor to generate a receptor potential in response to a stimulus.
FeatureReceptor potentialAction potential
AmplitudeGraded — proportional to stimulus strengthAll-or-none — cannot be graded
SpreadLocal, non-propagatedPropagated along the axon
SummationCan summate (spatial or temporal)Cannot be summated
TriggerDirect response to stimulus energyTriggered once receptor potentials summate to threshold

Multiple receptor potentials can build toward threshold in two ways:

  • Spatial summation — several neighbouring receptor sites are stimulated together and their potentials add up.
  • Temporal summation — one site is stimulated repeatedly in quick succession, and successive receptor potentials add up over time.

Once the combined potential reaches threshold, an action potential is triggered in the sensory neuron.

Worked example: the Pacinian corpuscle

Mechanism recap
Deep pressure on the Pacinian corpuscle → mechanical deformation opens Na⁺ channels → Na⁺ influx → local depolarization (the receptor potential) → local circuit current → summation → once threshold is reached at the first node of Ranvier, an action potential fires and propagates by saltatory conduction.
Properties 3 of 3

Adaptation

Definition
Adaptation is the decline of receptor-potential amplitude and action-potential frequency despite a constant stimulus intensity — in plain terms, "getting used to it."
Adaptation speedReceptor type nameExamplesEveryday analogy
RapidPhasic receptorsTouch receptorsYou stop feeling your clothes / a ring moments after putting them on
Moderate—Temperature receptorsA power cut feels intense at first, then you "get used to" the dark; a room's smell fades after a while
SlowTonic receptorsProprioceptorsProtective — lets you keep standing upright for hours without losing position sense
None / minimal—Pain receptors (nociceptors)You never fully "get used to" pain — an essential protective feature
Why pain must not adapt
Nociceptors show no or minimal adaptation — a critical protective mechanism ensuring the body keeps signalling ongoing tissue damage rather than "tuning it out."
Integration

Coding of Sensory Information

All sensations reach the brain as trains of action potentials — identical in form no matter the source. The brain discriminates four features of each sensation, much like a student ID encodes name, department, batch, and registration number:

1 · Modality

Every modality has its own specific adequate stimulus, specific receptor, specific afferent nerve, and specific cortical area.

Worked example: Taste
Adequate stimulusSweet, sour, bitter, salt
ReceptorsTaste buds — mucosa of epiglottis, palate, tongue, pharynx
AfferentsFacial (VII) · Glossopharyngeal (IX) · Vagus (X)
CentreThalamus & cerebral cortex

Two broad categories: Special senses (taste, smell, vision, hearing) vs. Somatic senses (pain, temperature, touch, pressure, vibration).

2 · Locality (Law of Projection)

The brain projects each incoming impulse back to the site of the originating receptor — the cerebral cortex has a "geographical map" where each area represents a different body part.

Phantom phenomena
When the sensory pathway is stimulated at any point along its course, the sensation is still felt at the site of the original receptor. This explains phantom limb pain (after amputation) and phantom tooth pain (after extraction) — the nerve pathway is stimulated, but the brain "projects" the sensation back to the tissue that no longer exists.

3 · Intensity

Weak vs. moderate vs. strong stimuli are distinguished by two variables:

  • The number of receptors stimulated (a pinprick excites few receptors; a knife wound recruits a whole row)
  • The frequency of action potentials generated

4 · Duration

The brain measures duration as the period from the onset to the end of receptor activation — a brief tap on the shoulder feels brief; sustained pressure for two hours is perceived as lasting two hours.

Vocabulary

TermMeaning
Sensory receptorSpecial structure at the peripheral/dendritic end of an afferent (sensory) neuron that detects a stimulus
Afferent neuronA neuron that carries impulses from the periphery toward the CNS
TransducerConverts a form of stimulus energy into a receptor potential
GeneratorConverts a receptor potential into an action potential
Receptor potentialLocal, non-propagated, graded electrical potential produced by a stimulated receptor
Action potentialAll-or-none, propagated electrical signal carried by the afferent neuron to the CNS

NociceptorPain receptor; sensitive to any stimulus causing tissue damage

ProprioceptorSenses position, movement, and rate of movement
Vestibular receptorNon-auditory inner-ear receptor for position, movement, and balance

Encapsulated receptorReceptor enclosed within a capsule (e.g. Pacinian, Meissner's)
Expanded tip receptorReceptor with an expanded (flattened) nerve ending (e.g. Merkel's discs, Ruffini endings)
Pacinian corpuscleEncapsulated receptor for deep pressure and fast vibration
Meissner's corpuscleEncapsulated receptor for slow vibration
Merkel's discsExpanded-tip receptor for sustained pressure and touch
Ruffini endingsExpanded-tip receptor for sustained pressure
TeleceptorDetects distant events (vision, hearing, smell)
ExteroceptorResponds to stimuli from outside the body
InteroceptorResponds to internal stimuli
SpecificityProperty whereby each receptor responds best to one adequate stimulus
ExcitabilityAbility of a receptor to generate a receptor potential in response to a stimulus
AdaptationDecline in receptor-potential amplitude and action-potential frequency despite constant stimulus intensity
Phasic receptorRapidly-adapting receptor (e.g. touch receptors)
Tonic receptorSlowly-adapting receptor (e.g. proprioceptors)
Spatial summationCombining receptor potentials from several neighbouring sites stimulated simultaneously
Temporal summationCombining successive receptor potentials from repeated stimulation over time at one site
Müller's law (law of specific nerve energies)Stimulation of a given sensory pathway always produces the one sensation that receptor is specialised for, regardless of the method of stimulation
Law of projectionThe brain always refers a sensation back to the site of the original receptor, regardless of where along the pathway it was stimulated
ModalityThe type of sensation (one of the four features coded by the brain)
LocalityThe site of a sensation
IntensityThe strength of a sensation, coded by number of receptors recruited and AP frequency
DurationHow long a sensation lasts, coded by the period of receptor activation
Phantom limb painPain felt in an amputated limb, explained by the law of projection
Phantom tooth painPain felt in an extracted tooth's socket, explained by the law of projection
Revision

High-Yield Exam Pearls

Pearl 1
Know the specific function and adequate stimulus for every receptor type: Pacinian corpuscle → deep pressure/fast vibration; Meissner's corpuscle → slow vibration; Merkel's discs → sustained pressure & touch; Ruffini endings → sustained pressure; Free nerve endings → pain & temperature. The lecturer explicitly stressed: "مطلوب منكم تعرفوا كل واحد مسؤول من شنو بيستقبل شنو."
Pearl 2
Understand the exception to the specificity rule: receptors can respond to stimuli other than their adequate stimulus if the threshold is extremely high — e.g. extreme pressure on a closed eye causing a sensation of light ("seeing stars").
Pearl 3
The adequate-stimulus rule does not strictly apply to pain receptors (nociceptors), because any form of energy can cause pain if it causes tissue damage.
Pearl 4
Müller's Law of specific nerve energies: the pathway from the receptor to the cortex is specific, and stimulation of that pathway always produces the one sensation for which the receptor is specialised.
Pearl 5
The Law of Projection explains why sensations are felt at the location of the receptor — heavily tested via phantom phenomena (phantom limb pain and phantom tooth pain).
Pearl 6
Receptor potentials are graded and local; action potentials are all-or-none and propagated. Only summation (spatial or temporal) of receptor potentials can trigger an action potential.
Pearl 7
Adaptation speed by receptor: Phasic (rapid) — touch; moderate — temperature; tonic (slow) — proprioceptors; none/minimal — pain (nociceptors).
Pearl 8
The brain codes every sensation using four features: Modality, Locality, Intensity, Duration. Intensity is coded by the number of receptors recruited and the frequency of action potentials, not by amplitude.
Revision

Clinical Pearls

Phantom Limb / Tooth Pain
After amputation or tooth extraction, a patient may still feel pain in the missing part because the sensory pathway to the cortex is stimulated, and the brain projects the sensation back to the original receptor site (Law of Projection).
Sensory Adaptation in Daily Life
Phasic receptors adapt rapidly (e.g. losing the sensation of clothes or a ring shortly after putting them on). Tonic receptors adapt slowly (e.g. proprioceptors keeping you balanced while standing for long periods without falling).
Pain Receptors Do Not Adapt
Nociceptors have minimal to no adaptation, serving as a critical protective mechanism so the body continues to recognise ongoing tissue damage.
High-Threshold Sensation
Extreme mechanical pressure on the eye can bypass standard specificity and trigger visual receptors (seeing "stars") — a useful bedside conceptualisation of overriding the adequate-stimulus threshold.
Stimulus Intensity & Tissue Damage
The clinical intensity of a stimulus (e.g. a pinprick vs. a knife wound) is determined by the number of receptors stimulated and the frequency of the generated action potentials.
